title: Social Security and Other Legislation Amendment (Income Support for Students) Bill 2009

divisions.question: That the motion ( **Mr Pyne’s** ) be agreed to.
Judi Moylan The question is that the bill be agreed to. Question put.
That the amendment ( **Senator Hanson-Young’s** ) be agreed to.
That Senate amendments Nos 1 and 2 be agreed to. That Senate amendments Nos 3 to 9 be disagreed to. That the motion ( **Ms Gillard’s** ) be agreed to.

That the House has agreed to amendments Nos (1) and (2) made by the Senate and disagreed to amendments Nos (3) to (9), and requesting the reconsideration of those amendments disagreed to. That the committee does not insist on the Senate amendments to which the House has disagreed.
That the amendments ( **Senator Carr’s** ) be agreed to.
That the report from the committee be adopted. That the report from the committee be adopted.

speeches.speaker: John Faulkner
speeches.brief: The bill implements the Government’s response to the Bradley Review, reforming student income support to better target those most in need. Key measures include lowering the Youth Allowance automatic independence age from 25 to 22, raising the parental income test threshold to $44,165, introducing student start-up scholarships of $2,254 a year and relocation scholarships of $1,000 a year ($4,000 initially), and exempting merit and equity scholarships from the income test up to $6,762 a year.

speeches.speaker: Brett Mason
speeches.brief: The coalition announced it will move four amendments to the bill to remove retrospectivity for 30,000 affected gap-year students and retain a rural workforce participation pathway for Youth Allowance, funded by reducing the student start-up scholarship from $2,254 to $1,000 per year. The speaker argued the bill’s tightening of workforce participation criteria will harm rural, regional and remote students who rely on gap-year earnings to afford university, contradicting the government’s stated aim of increasing access for disadvantaged groups.

speeches.speaker: Michael Ronaldson
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the government's changes to youth allowance eligibility would force rural and regional students to defer study for two years, disadvantaging them compared to city students. He cited a 1992 example of parents choosing which child could attend university, and stated that 25,000 gap-year students would be affected by the retrospective changes.

Senator Hanson-Young moved an amendment to the bill's second reading motion, calling on the Government to increase the 2010-11 Budget so that Youth Allowance matches Newstart, which provides a maximum fortnightly payment of $456.

speeches.speaker: Ian Macdonald
speeches.brief: The bill's supporters argued for amendments to better assist rural and regional students, citing evidence that students at James Cook University spend roughly $10,500 per year and 70% receive family support. The coalition proposed delaying the new workforce participation criteria from 1 January 2010 to 1 January 2011 and removing retrospectivity for students in a gap year.

speeches.speaker: Kim Carr
speeches.brief: The government opposed amendments to the Social Security and Other Legislation Amendment (Income Support for Students) Bill 2009 that would have created a 100-kilometre relocation rule, a 90-minute travel criterion, or a "required to live away from home" test for youth allowance independence, citing budget costs of up to $750 million. The opposition, Greens and Family First supported various versions of these amendments, arguing the bill disadvantaged rural and regional students who must relocate for university.

speeches.speaker: Julian McGauran
speeches.brief: The opposition moved amendments to extend the gap year transition period for youth allowance independence until 31 December 2010 or 1 January 2011, and to reduce the student start-up scholarship from $2,254 to $1,000 per year to fund the extension, arguing the government's changes were retrospectively unfair to students who had been advised to take a gap year.
The House agreed to Senate amendments (1) and (2) but disagreed to amendments (3) through (9), requesting the Senate reconsider the rejected amendments.

speeches.speaker: Ursula Stephens
speeches.brief: The coalition opposed the government's motion, insisting on two non-negotiable amendments: protecting 30,000 gap year students from retrospectivity and creating an extra pathway for rural students who must leave home to study. They offered to split the legislation to preserve start-up scholarships for 150,000 students in 2010.

speeches.speaker: Kim Carr
speeches.brief: The government moved to adopt a committee report, arguing that failure would leave 150,000 students without scholarships or support in 2010. The opposition and Senator Fielding opposed the motion, citing unmet demands for retrospectivity and a rural student pathway.
